cards.back: ΔH for the doubled equation also doubles.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What happens to ΔH if a reaction is reversed?
cards.back: The enthalpy sign reverses.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What equation relates heat, mass, specific heat capacity and temperature rise?
cards.back: q=mcΔT with q in J, m in g, c in J g⁻¹ K⁻¹.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How is ΔT calculated from initial and final temperatures?
cards.back: ΔT=T_final−T_initial; changes in °C and K are numerically equal.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: When liquid density is 1 g cm⁻³, how does mass relate to volume?
cards.back: Solution mass in grams approximately equals its volume in cm³.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: In a solution calorimeter, what mass usually goes in q=mcΔT?
cards.back: Mass of the solution that changes temperature, not only the solute.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How do you convert calorimetry q from J into kJ?
cards.back: Divide by 1000.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How do you calculate reaction molar ΔH using solution q?
cards.back: ΔH=−q_solution(kJ)/moles of reaction, with sign chosen correctly.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why is ΔH negative if the solution warms?
cards.back: The solution gains heat, so the reaction has released it.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why is ΔH positive if the solution cools?
cards.back: The solution loses heat; the reaction absorbs heat from surroundings.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why must a reaction mole ratio be checked before finding molar ΔH?
cards.back: The enthalpy is defined per mole of reaction as written; reactants may have unequal ratios.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: For 25 cm³ 1 M HCl plus 25 cm³ 1 M NaOH, how many mol water form?
cards.back: 0.025 mol, assuming complete 1:1 neutralisation.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the purpose of a calorimeter's insulation?
cards.back: To reduce heat transfer between system and external surroundings.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What happens to the measured magnitude of exothermic ΔH if heat escapes?
cards.back: The temperature rise is too small; calculated ΔH is less negative.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What happens when an endothermic experiment gains external heat?
cards.back: Temperature fall is too small; measured ΔH is underestimated in magnitude.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why might a fuel combustion calorimetry estimate be too weak?
cards.back: Some heat escapes or warms apparatus, so measured water rise is too small.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why can incomplete combustion affect fuel calorimetry?
cards.back: Not all fuel undergoes the stated complete combustion reaction.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does extrapolating a temperature–time graph estimate?
cards.back: Corrected temperature at the mixing/reaction time, reducing heat-exchange error.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What are possible uncertainties in simple calorimetry?
cards.back: Temperature resolution, mass/volume accuracy and imperfect insulation.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Does AQA require the specific heat capacity of water from memory?
cards.back: No; the value is supplied when needed.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: State Hess's law.
cards.back: Overall enthalpy change is independent of pathway if start/end states match.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the formation-enthalpy calculation for ΔH°reaction?
cards.back: Sum of product ΔfH° values minus sum of reactant ΔfH° values.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the combustion-enthalpy Hess calculation?
cards.back: Sum combustion enthalpies of reactants minus those of products.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why do equation coefficients matter in Hess calculations?
cards.back: Multiply each substance's molar enthalpy by its stoichiometric coefficient.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What happens to a Hess enthalpy when an equation is reversed?
cards.back: Change the sign.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What happens to a Hess enthalpy when the equation is halved?
cards.back: Halve the ΔH value.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why is the ΔfH° of H₂(g) zero?
cards.back: Hydrogen gas is elemental hydrogen in its standard state.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: In a formation cycle, what is the common lower pathway?
cards.back: Both reactants and products can be related to the same constituent elements.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: In a combustion cycle, what common products can both pathways reach?
cards.back: Complete combustion products, typically CO₂(g) and H₂O(l).

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why can Hess's law calculate a reaction not measured directly?
cards.back: A sum of accessible reactions can have the same overall initial and final states.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What cycle relation holds if X→solution is ΔH1 and hydrate→solution is ΔH2?
cards.back: X→hydrate ΔH=ΔH1−ΔH2, with all states/amounts matching.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How can enthalpies of solution determine hydration of a salt?
cards.back: Construct paths to the same aqueous final state; subtract the two dissolution ΔHs.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Define mean bond enthalpy.
cards.back: Average enthalpy to break 1 mol of a stated covalent bond in gaseous molecules.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the general bond-enthalpy estimate for reaction ΔH?
cards.back: Sum of energies for bonds broken − sum of energies for bonds formed.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the sign of bond breaking?
cards.back: Positive (endothermic): energy is required.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the sign of bond formation?
cards.back: Negative contribution (exothermic): energy is released.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why must you count all bonds in the balanced equation?
cards.back: Coefficients determine the number of each bond broken and formed.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Are mean bond enthalpies exact for a specific compound?
cards.back: No; they are averages across different molecular environments.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why can mean bond-enthalpy ΔH differ from standard experimental ΔH?
cards.back: Mean gas-phase energies are approximate and actual substances may have other states.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why is liquid water a problem if only gas-phase mean bonds are used?
cards.back: Condensation/phase enthalpy is omitted unless accounted for.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Does an exothermic reaction always break fewer bonds than it forms?
cards.back: No; total energies of breaking and forming matter, not simple bond count.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is a bond enthalpy calculation not suitable for without extra data?
cards.back: Directly predicting full ΔH for non-gaseous substances without state corrections.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is AQA Required Practical 2 about?
cards.back: Measuring an enthalpy change using calorimetry.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Give examples of AQA RP2 reaction types.
cards.back: Dissolving salts, neutralisation, displacement and combustion calorimetry.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why might a polystyrene cup and lid be used in calorimetry?
cards.back: To limit heat transfer to the outside and reduce evaporation.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why should a temperature–time correction be considered?
cards.back: Heat exchange can distort the measured maximum/minimum temperature.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What must be explained in a good calorimetry evaluation?
cards.back: Direction of error, its cause, impact on ΔT/ΔH and a realistic improvement.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why might dissolving hydrated vs anhydrous salts help build a Hess cycle?
cards.back: Two measurable solution enthalpies lead to a common final aqueous state.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: A thermometer is ±0.1°C per reading. What is the uncertainty in ΔT?
cards.back: ±0.2°C: add the absolute uncertainties of initial and final readings.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: For ΔT=6.0°C and ±0.1°C per reading, what is % uncertainty?

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How can a slow thermometer affect exothermic calorimetry?
cards.back: It may miss the highest temperature; ΔT is too small and ΔH less negative.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why is 2H₂(g)+O₂(g)→2H₂O(l) not a one-mole formation equation?
cards.back: It forms 2 mol H₂O; halve every coefficient for standard molar formation.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why are tabulated H–Cl bond enthalpies approximate for H₂+Cl₂→2HCl?
cards.back: Tabulated values can be rounded; diatomic HCl has one fixed bond environment.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the formula and charge of sulfate?
cards.back: SO₄²⁻, charge −2.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the formula and charge of hydroxide?
cards.back: OH⁻, charge −1.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the formula and charge of nitrate?
cards.back: NO₃⁻, charge −1.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the formula and charge of carbonate?
cards.back: CO₃²⁻, charge −2.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the formula and charge of ammonium?
cards.back: NH₄⁺, charge +1.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the formula of aluminium nitrate?
cards.back: Al(NO₃)₃: one Al³⁺ balances three NO₃⁻.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the formula of ammonium sulfate?
cards.back: (NH₄)₂SO₄: two NH₄⁺ balance SO₄²⁻.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the formula of magnesium nitrate?
cards.back: Mg(NO₃)₂: Mg²⁺ balances two NO₃⁻.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why must ionic formulae have balanced charges?
cards.back: A compound is neutral: total positive and negative charges sum to zero.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: First step for an unfamiliar molecular-shape question?
cards.back: Draw a Lewis structure, identifying the central atom and its bonding and lone pairs.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How are double and triple bonds counted in VSEPR?
cards.back: Each multiple bond is one region of electron density around the central atom.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What decides a molecule's shape rather than electron geometry?
cards.back: Positions of atoms/bonding regions; lone pairs affect angles but are not named as vertices.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why are lone-pair repulsions stronger than bond-pair repulsions?
cards.back: Lone-pair electron density is closer to the central atom and repels bonding pairs more.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What electron-domain shape results from three domains?
cards.back: Trigonal planar, approximately 120° before lone-pair distortion.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Three electron domains: 2 bonds and 1 lone pair. Shape?
cards.back: Bent (V-shaped), with a bond angle slightly below 120°.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Four electron domains: 2 bonds and 2 lone pairs. Shape?
cards.back: Bent, around 104.5° in H₂O.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Four electron domains: 3 bonds and 1 lone pair. Shape?
cards.back: Trigonal pyramidal, about 107° in NH₃.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Four electron domains: 4 bonds and no lone pairs. Shape?
cards.back: Tetrahedral, about 109.5°.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Five electron domains without lone pairs: shape and angles?
cards.back: Trigonal bipyramidal: 90°, 120° and 180°.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why do lone pairs prefer equatorial sites in a trigonal bipyramid?
cards.back: Fewer 90° interactions, so lone-pair repulsion is reduced.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Five domains: 3 bonds, 2 lone pairs. Shape?
cards.back: T-shaped (e.g. ClF₃), with two equatorial lone pairs.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Five domains: 2 bonds, 3 lone pairs. Shape?
cards.back: Linear (e.g. XeF₂); three lone pairs occupy equatorial sites.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Six domains: 5 bonds and 1 lone pair. Shape?
cards.back: Square pyramidal (e.g. BrF₅), approximately 90° angles.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Six domains: 4 bonds and 2 lone pairs. Shape?
cards.back: Square planar (e.g. XeF₄); lone pairs opposite each other.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why are H₂O bond angles smaller than those in NH₃?
cards.back: H₂O has two lone pairs rather than one, so the bonding pairs are pushed closer together.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What must a full 4-mark molecular-shape explanation include?
cards.back: Electron domains, lone-pair count, repulsion order, shape and approximate bond angle.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How do you identify δ+ and δ− in a polar bond?
cards.back: More electronegative atom is δ−; the other atom is δ+.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Are polar bonds sufficient for a molecular permanent dipole?
cards.back: No; the bond dipoles must not cancel when the 3D shape is considered.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Compare the permanent dipoles of CO₂ and SO₂.
cards.back: CO₂: none, linear dipoles cancel. SO₂: present, bent dipoles do not cancel.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why is NH₃ a polar molecule?
cards.back: N–H bonds are polar and trigonal pyramidal shape prevents cancellation.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why does CHCl₃ have a permanent dipole but CCl₄ does not?
cards.back: CHCl₃ is asymmetrical; CCl₄ is symmetrical with cancelling C–Cl dipoles.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Can a non-polar molecule contain polar bonds? Example?
cards.back: Yes. In BF₃ the three polar B–F bond dipoles cancel.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What are the two checks for molecular polarity?
cards.back: Check electronegativity differences in bonds, then whether the 3D dipoles cancel.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How do bond polarities differ from intermolecular forces?
cards.back: Bond polarity concerns uneven sharing within a bond; intermolecular forces act between molecules.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What name does your class use for induced dipole–dipole attractions?
cards.back: Van der Waals' forces (induced dipole–dipole attractions).

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What causes van der Waals' forces?
cards.back: Temporary electron fluctuations make dipoles that induce dipoles in neighbouring particles.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Do non-polar molecules experience van der Waals' forces?
cards.back: Yes; induced dipoles form even without a permanent molecular dipole.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why are van der Waals' forces stronger in I₂ than Cl₂?
cards.back: I₂ has more electrons and a more easily polarised cloud, making stronger induced dipoles.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How do stronger van der Waals' forces affect boiling point?
cards.back: More energy is needed to separate molecules, so the boiling point increases.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why is water's boiling point anomalously high?
cards.back: O–H polarity allows H bonds between δ+ H and a lone pair on O of another molecule.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why does HF hydrogen bond strongly but HCl not normally?
cards.back: In HF, H is bonded to F; in HCl, H is bonded to Cl, not N, O or F.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is overcome when iodine boils: I–I bonds or van der Waals' forces?
cards.back: Intermolecular van der Waals' forces; I–I covalent bonds stay intact.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: In boiling water, which bonds stay intact?
cards.back: The covalent O–H bonds; intermolecular hydrogen bonds are overcome.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How should a four-mark ionic melting-point answer be built?
cards.back: State giant ionic lattice, opposite-ion electrostatic forces, strong attractions, much energy.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Give the 4-step structure of a halogen boiling-point explanation.
cards.back: Non-polar; more electrons; stronger induced dipoles/van der Waals' forces; more energy to boil.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How should a four-mark bond-polarity comparison be built?
cards.back: Identify polar bonds, δ charges, 3D shapes, then cancel/non-cancel bond dipoles.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How should you justify a lower bond angle in a 4-mark answer?
cards.back: Count bond/lone pairs, compare repulsions, name shape and resulting reduced angle.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Four-mark plan: why does one liquid hydrogen-bond more strongly?
cards.back: Identify N/O/F–H bond, δ+ H, acceptor lone pair, and energy needed to separate molecules.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What pressure is used for AQA standard enthalpy changes?
cards.back: 100 kPa.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Must a standard enthalpy change always be at 298 K?
cards.back: No; a stated temperature is required, often 298 K.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does 'standard state' mean in enthalpy definitions?
cards.back: The most stable physical form of a substance at the specified conditions.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Name standard states of water, bromine and carbon at 298 K.
cards.back: H₂O(l), Br₂(l), C(s, graphite).

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What must a standard enthalpy of formation equation produce?
cards.back: Exactly 1 mol of compound from its elements in standard states.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What must a standard enthalpy of combustion equation consume?
cards.back: Exactly 1 mol of substance, burned completely in O₂.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the definition of Hess's law?
cards.back: Reaction enthalpy is route-independent if initial/final states are the same.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the molar enthalpy formula if q_solution is in joules?
cards.back: ΔH = −q_solution/(1000 × n) in kJ mol⁻¹.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does n mean in ΔH = −q/n?
cards.back: Moles of the reaction as written, or of the species named in the definition.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why is there a minus sign in ΔH = −q_solution/n?
cards.back: Heat gained by solution equals heat lost by reaction (and vice versa).

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: When finding q=mcΔT, do equation coefficients multiply m?
cards.back: No. m is the mass of material undergoing the temperature change.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What must you do to q in joules before obtaining kJ mol⁻¹?
cards.back: Divide q by 1000, then by the appropriate moles.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: If 2 mol of A react per equation, what is n_reaction from 0.10 mol A?
cards.back: 0.10 ÷ 2 = 0.050 mol of reaction as written.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: In H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O, 0.040 mol NaOH is how many reactions?
cards.back: 0.040 ÷ 2 = 0.020 mol of the equation as written.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: For neutralisation enthalpy per mole of water, which n do you use?
cards.back: Moles of H₂O made, not automatically moles of acid or alkali.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What tells you whether to use n of reactant, product or reaction?
cards.back: The stated definition of ΔH and coefficients in the balanced equation.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: For ΔfH° values, which subtraction order gives reaction ΔH?
cards.back: Sum of products − sum of reactants, including coefficients.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: For ΔcH° values, which subtraction order gives reaction ΔH?
cards.back: Sum of reactants − sum of products, including coefficients.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: For 2CO + O₂ → 2CO₂, how many times each ΔfH°?
cards.back: CO₂ ×2, CO ×2, O₂ ×1; ΔfH°(O₂)=0.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: When should you multiply a Hess enthalpy by 2?
cards.back: When the corresponding chemical equation is doubled.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What happens to ΔH when you reverse a Hess equation?
cards.back: Change the sign of ΔH.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What happens to ΔH when you halve every equation coefficient?
cards.back: Halve ΔH for that equation.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How do you check Hess arrows if the formula is forgotten?
cards.back: Follow start → finish through the cycle; reverse arrow = reverse sign.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why is ΔfH° of O₂(g) zero at 298 K?
cards.back: O₂(g) is oxygen's element in its standard state.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: When are Hess reaction coefficients NOT extra multipliers?
cards.back: If a supplied ΔH already belongs to the full balanced equation shown.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: In bond enthalpy sums, do you multiply by formula subscripts?
cards.back: Count bonds in each molecule, then multiply by the equation coefficient.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: For 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, how many O–H bonds form?
cards.back: 4 O–H bonds: 2 water molecules ×2 bonds each.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: In hydrogenation of ethene, what happens to unchanged C–H bonds?
cards.back: They cancel between reactants and products; count only the net changes.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is AQA Required Practical 2?
cards.back: Measurement of an enthalpy change using calorimetry.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why does a polystyrene cup help in solution calorimetry?
cards.back: It reduces heat transfer between the solution and surroundings.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why can a lid improve a calorimetry experiment?
cards.back: It reduces heat exchange with surroundings and evaporation.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is the key graph correction in exothermic calorimetry?
cards.back: Extrapolate post-reaction cooling to mixing time to estimate peak T.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What effect does heat loss have on calculated exothermic ΔH?
cards.back: Measured ΔT is too small, so ΔH is less negative than the true value.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What does thermometer ±0.1°C mean for a temperature difference?
cards.back: Two readings give ±0.2°C absolute uncertainty in ΔT.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What practical details matter beyond Paper 3?
cards.back: Apparatus, temperature change, controls, uncertainties, errors and improvements.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Which parts of RP2 affect the calorimetry calculation directly?
cards.back: Measured ΔT, solution mass, heat capacity and reaction moles.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Displacement–time: what does a negative gradient mean?
cards.back: Velocity is negative: motion in the negative direction, not necessarily slowing down.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What does zero gradient on a displacement–time graph show?
cards.back: Zero velocity: stationary at that instant or throughout a flat segment.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: On a velocity–time graph, what does an area below the axis mean?
cards.back: Negative displacement; add its magnitude when calculating total distance.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Why is total distance different from displacement on a v–t graph?
cards.back: Distance sums all absolute areas; displacement uses signed areas.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: A straight sloping v–t line crosses zero. What changes?
cards.back: Direction changes if velocity changes sign; speed falls to zero then rises.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Acceleration–time area gives which quantity?
cards.back: Change in velocity, not displacement or distance.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: For curved s–t graphs, how is instantaneous velocity found?
cards.back: Find the gradient of the tangent at that time.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: How do you identify acceleration on a v–t graph?
cards.back: Gradient Δv/Δt; a horizontal line means zero acceleration.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: On a 30° slope, which component of weight pulls downhill?
cards.back: mg sin30°; the perpendicular component is mg cos30°.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: A horizontal push up a slope does what to the reaction?
cards.back: It adds a component into the surface, increasing the normal reaction.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What is the moment of two equal opposite forces forming a couple?
cards.back: One force × perpendicular separation of their lines of action.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: What does the gradient of a displacement vs t² graph give in free fall?
cards.back: g/2, for release from rest with negligible drag.
